name: Hvannadalshnúkur, Iceland's highest peak
why: The longest summit day in Europe: from almost sea level to 2,110 m, roped together across the snow of the Öræfajökull caldera, with the whole Vatnajökull ice cap to the north.
book: Only with a licensed mountain guide and a rope team. Guided climbs start from Sandfell (on Route 1 south-east of Skaftafell) in the season, usually April to August and shorter in recent years; a briefing at the Skaftafell base at 16:00 the day before. Keep spare days for the weather.
water: One stream on the way up to refill; carry 3 litres of capacity and food for 14 hours.
dangers: Hidden crevasses under the snow on the upper half: rope, harness and a guide who knows the unmarked line.
Whiteout and storm on the caldera; the weather decides most attempts.
Over 2,000 m of climb in one day: exhaustion on the way down, and the team turns back together.
Snow blindness and sunburn on the snow: glacier glasses and sun cream.
turnaround: The guide turns the team when the day would pass 16 hours, or in whiteout or wind. Above 700 m the whole rope team stays together.

points.name: Sandfell trailhead
points.note: The old farm and church site of Sandfell by Route 1, about 100 m above the sea. The path climbs straight up the Sandfellsheiði ridge, in the dark at the start.

points.name: Snow line on Sandfellsheiði
points.note: Around 1,000-1,100 m the rock path ends on the snow: crampons and harness on, the rope team ties in here.

points.name: Öræfajökull caldera
points.note: Around 1,800 m on the rim: the long white crossing of the ice-filled crater, with the summit pyramid ahead.

points.name: Hvannadalshnúkur summit
points.note: 2,110 m, the highest point in Iceland. The last steep slope is often done with axe and crampons. Return the same way.
